title: London Festival Celebrates Northeast India's Rich Culture as Diaspora Builds Community Abroad
excerpt: The 'United Colours of North East India' event at the Indian Gymkhana Club brought together communities from all eight northeastern states for a day-long celebration of food, performance, and heritage.
body:
• The 'United Colours of North East India' festival held on July 11 at London's Indian Gymkhana Club showcased traditions from all eight northeastern states — Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram, Tripura, Arunachal Pradesh, and Sikkim.
  • The event featured cultural performances, traditional attire showcases, handicraft stalls, authentic regional food, and family-friendly activities across a nine-and-a-half-hour program.
  • The festival was organized by North East Indians In UK, a community group working to preserve and promote northeastern Indian heritage among the diaspora in Britain.
  • The celebration comes amid growing visibility of the NE Indian diaspora in the UK, coinciding with South Asian Heritage Month activities across London.

A Day of Cultural Immersion

The Indian Gymkhana Club in Osterley, west London, transformed into a vibrant showcase of northeastern Indian culture on July 11 as the 'United Colours of North East India' festival drew members of the diaspora from across the United Kingdom.

The all-day event, running from 12:30 p.m. to 10 p.m., brought together communities representing all eight northeastern Indian states under one roof. Attendees experienced cultural performances, traditional attire showcases, and art workshops alongside stalls selling handicrafts and handloom textiles from the region.

Food, Music, and Community Pride

Authentic regional food from across the northeast — spanning Assamese thalis, Manipuri snacks, Naga specialties, and more — drew long lines throughout the day. The culinary showcase doubled as an education in the region's diverse food traditions, many of which remain underrepresented even within India's broader culinary landscape.

The festival's headline act, The Confidentials, performed a wide-ranging setlist spanning decades of popular music, while a DJ kept the energy going between cultural segments. Traditional dance performances and attire showcases highlighted the distinct identities of each state's communities.

Family-friendly activities included art workshops, a three-piece obstacle course, and a bouncy castle, drawing multi-generational attendance.

Building Diaspora Networks

The event was organized by North East Indians In UK, a community group that has worked to create spaces for cultural connection and preservation among the growing northeastern Indian population in Britain.

Northeastern Indians have historically been one of the less visible segments of the Indian diaspora in the UK, with community organizations centered primarily around Bengali, Gujarati, Punjabi, and Tamil populations. Events like 'United Colours of North East India' aim to change that dynamic by creating dedicated platforms for the region's diverse communities.

The festival took place during South Asian Heritage Month in the UK, which has seen a growing calendar of Indian cultural events across London this summer. It also followed the London Indian Film Festival, where the Mumbai International Film Festival's North East India showcase highlighted filmmakers from the region.

Northeast India's Growing Global Footprint

The festival reflects a broader trend of northeastern Indian communities establishing stronger cultural networks abroad. In India, the northeast has gained visibility through events like the North East India Film Festival and the Masala Festival in Newcastle, which celebrated its 10th year of South Asian arts programming in 2026.

For second-generation members of the diaspora, events like the London festival serve as a bridge to cultural traditions that can fade in migration — from Bihu dance to Naga weaving techniques to Khasi music traditions.

The Indian Gymkhana Club, one of the oldest Indian clubs in Britain founded in 1916, provided a fitting venue for the celebration, connecting the history of Indian community life in the UK with its evolving cultural landscape.
